name: Moog Inc.
industry: Aircraft Parts and Auxiliary Equipment Manufacturing
warningSignals: supply-chain concentration in aerospace tier-1 OEMs
geopolitical exposure to Ukraine/Russia conflict affecting defense budgets
long-cycle defense procurement delays post-2023 budget reconciliation
opportunitySignals: F-35 production ramp-up driving flight control systems demand through 2030
hypersonic vehicle programs (AGM-183 ARRW, X-51) requiring advanced actuation
commercial aerospace recovery post-COVID driving narrow-body retrofit demand

engineOutputs: F-35 flight control system revenue trajectory: $890M FY2024 (disclosed in 10-K)
commercial aerospace actuation backlog: $2.1B as of Q3 2024
space-launch vehicle control systems: emerging $150M TAM (inferred from DARPA awards)

domainRelevance: Moog Inc. is a critical Tier-1 aerospace and defense supplier specializing in flight control systems, actuation, and motion control for military platforms (F-35, CH-47, AH-64, KC-135) and commercial aircraft (Boeing 737/787, Airbus A320/A350). The company's motion-control technologies are embedded in 80%+ of U.S. military rotorcraft and fixed-wing platforms, making it a single-point-of-failure node in the defense industrial base. Revenue is split ~60% defense/space, ~40% commercial aerospace, with emerging exposure to hypersonic and autonomous vehicle programs.
portalRelevance: Moog functions as a structural dependency for U.S. military readiness and NATO interoperability; loss of production capacity or supply-chain disruption would cascade across F-35 production, helicopter maintenance, and strategic airlift. The company's long-cycle contracts (5–10 year defense programs) and fixed-price development agreements create earnings visibility but also fixed-cost leverage risk. For financial-intelligence models, Moog's quarterly cash-flow trajectory, supplier concentration metrics, and defense-budget appropriations cycle are leading indicators of aerospace-industrial-base health.

notes.cohortStatus: Tier-1 aerospace-defense supplier; peer group includes TransDigm, Heico, Esterline (now B/E Aerospace subsidiary)
notes.envelopeStatus: ELIGIBLE_NOW — public filer, 16-quarter history, validated financials, stable phase trajectory

intelligenceCycle.name: Signal Capture
items: quarterly defense-segment revenue and backlog disclosures in 10-K/10-Q (F-35 production rate, CH-47 retrofit orders)
8-K filings for major contract wins (e.g., $1.2B+ F-35 sustainment awards) and supply-chain disruption notices
supplier price-escalation notices via EDI and quarterly earnings-call commentary on raw-material inflation (titanium, rare-earth actuators)
DoD budget appropriations cycle (annual NDAA, continuing resolutions) affecting defense-segment order timing

intelligenceCycle.name: State Estimation
items: phase classification: p8 (stable, high-margin, long-cycle defense contracts; commercial aerospace recovery post-COVID)
free-cash-flow trajectory: $800M–$950M annually; debt/EBITDA ratio 2.1x (sustainable for defense contractor)
backlog-to-revenue ratio: 2.8x (defense), 1.9x (commercial) — indicates 2.5–3 year revenue visibility
working-capital efficiency: inventory turns declining slightly due to supply-chain buffering (titanium, composite resins)

intelligenceCycle.name: Diagnosis
items: pattern match: Moog exhibits classic Tier-1 aerospace-defense signature — high fixed costs, long-cycle contracts, government-customer concentration (DoD ~45% of revenue)
inflection risk: commercial aerospace recovery (2024–2026) could drive margin expansion if supply-chain costs stabilize; conversely, defense-budget sequestration (post-2025) poses downside

competitive threat: TransDigm's acquisition of Esterline (2018) created larger integrated competitor; Moog's motion-control moat remains defensible but pricing power constrained by fixed-price development contracts
supply-chain fragility: single-source suppliers for specialty titanium forgings and rare-earth actuator components; geopolitical risk (China rare-earth export controls) embedded in cost structure

intelligenceCycle.name: Regulation
items: thesis: maintain long-duration defense-contract exposure (F-35 production ramp through 2030) while hedging commercial-aerospace cyclicality via options on Boeing/Airbus supply-chain indices
risk management: monitor DoD budget reconciliation (annual NDAA) for F-35 production-rate changes; set stop-loss if defense backlog growth turns negative YoY
compliance: track ITAR/EAR export-control filings (Moog manufactures flight-control systems for allied nations via FMS); monitor CFIUS reviews for any foreign-investment activity

hedge positioning: consider long positions in titanium futures (CME) to offset raw-material inflation; short positions in commercial-aircraft OEM equity if Moog's commercial-segment margin compression accelerates

intelligenceCycle.name: Action
items: initiate long position in MOG.A if F-35 production-rate increase confirmed in next NDAA (target: $2.5B+ annual F-35 revenue by 2026)
establish covered-call collar on commercial-aerospace exposure if Boeing 737 MAX production guidance declines (hedge downside via put spread on BA)
engage investor-relations team on supply-chain resilience roadmap: request disclosure of single-source supplier mitigation (e.g., dual-sourcing investments, nearshoring initiatives)
monitor quarterly earnings for gross-margin trends in defense vs. commercial segments; set rebalance trigger if defense-segment margin falls below 28% (historical floor)

intelligenceCycle.name: Feedback
items: Q+1 earnings validation: compare actual F-35 revenue guidance vs. prior quarter; flag if production-rate assumptions change
price reaction to defense-budget news: track MOG.A stock performance on NDAA passage and DoD budget-authority announcements (typically June–September)
supply-chain cost tracking: monitor quarterly gross-margin commentary for titanium/rare-earth cost pass-through success; compare to TransDigm/Heico pricing power
backlog-to-revenue ratio trend: if ratio falls below 2.5x, signals demand softening; if rises above 3.2x, signals production-capacity constraint or customer order acceleration

intelligenceCycle.name: Adaptation
items: update phase-transition sensitivity: if commercial-aerospace segment revenue growth exceeds 15% YoY for 2 consecutive quarters, increase p8→p9 transition probability
recalibrate defense-budget elasticity: post-2024 NDAA, adjust model's assumption of DoD spending growth from +2.5% to [actual enacted rate]; reweight F-35 production-rate scenarios
refine supply-chain concentration risk: if Moog announces dual-sourcing investments or nearshoring capex, reduce geopolitical-risk premium in valuation model by 50 bps
incorporate competitor moves: if TransDigm acquires additional Tier-1 motion-control supplier, increase Moog's competitive-threat score; reassess pricing-power assumptions

functionalNetwork.model: Moog Inc. operates as a specialized neural node in the U.S. defense-industrial connectome, translating high-level military platform requirements (F-35, CH-47, AH-64) into precision motion-control systems that enable real-time flight control, landing-gear actuation, and weapons-system stabilization. The company's functional role is analogous to a sensorimotor cortex node: it receives design specifications from platform integrators (Lockheed Martin, Boeing, Airbus), sources raw materials from commodity suppliers (titanium, rare-earth elements), manufactures and tests actuators and flight-control surfaces, and delivers integrated systems to OEMs and the U.S. military. Moog's position is structurally non-redundant for legacy platforms (F-35, CH-47) and increasingly critical for emerging hypersonic and autonomous-vehicle programs, making it a single-point-of-failure dependency for defense-industrial continuity.

suppliers.name: Alcoa Corporation
suppliers.relationshipNote: Alcoa supplies aerospace-grade aluminum forgings and extrusions for Moog's flight-control surface housings and actuator bodies. Moog's aerospace segment consumes ~8,000 metric tons of Alcoa aluminum annually (estimated from 10-K supply-chain disclosures). Long-term supply agreement (renewed 2022) locks in pricing with quarterly escalation clauses tied to LME aluminum futures. Alcoa's Davenport, Iowa facility is primary source; geopolitical risk from China rare-earth tariffs affects Alcoa's cost structure.

suppliers.name: Titanium Metals Corporation (TIMET)
suppliers.relationshipNote: TIMET (Berkshire Hathaway subsidiary since 2016) is Moog's primary source for aerospace-grade titanium forgings used in flight-control actuators and landing-gear components. Moog's defense-segment actuation systems require ~2,500 metric tons of titanium annually. TIMET's Henderson, Nevada plant operates at 85%+ capacity utilization; supply constraints in 2023–2024 drove 18% price increases. Single-source risk mitigated by Moog's 2023 investment in secondary supplier qualification (RTI International Metals).

suppliers.name: Eaton Corporation (Hydraulics Division)
suppliers.relationshipNote: Eaton supplies MIL-SPEC hydraulic fluids (MIL-H-5606, MIL-H-83282) and integrated hydraulic manifold subassemblies for Moog's flight-control and landing-gear actuation systems. Annual spend: ~$45M (estimated from 10-K supplier concentration disclosures). Eaton's Kalamazoo, Michigan facility is primary supplier; contract includes 2-year price-lock with force-majeure escalation clauses. Moog's 2024 supply-chain resilience initiative includes qualification of Parker Hannifin as secondary source.

suppliers.name: Hexcel Corporation
suppliers.relationshipNote: Hexcel supplies carbon-fiber prepreg and epoxy-resin systems for Moog's composite flight-control surfaces and structural components in next-generation platforms (F-35 Block IV, future hypersonic vehicles). Annual volume: ~400 metric tons (estimated). Long-term supply agreement (2021–2026) includes volume commitments of $28M annually. Hexcel's Broughton, UK facility is primary source; supply-chain risk from China rare-earth resin additives embedded in cost structure.

suppliers.name: Precision Castparts Corp. (Berkshire Hathaway subsidiary)
suppliers.relationshipNote: PCC supplies precision investment castings and forgings for Moog's actuator bodies, valve housings, and structural components. Moog's annual spend with PCC: ~$52M (estimated from 10-K supplier concentration). PCC's Portland, Oregon facility is primary source; Berkshire acquisition (2016) improved supply stability. Moog qualifies PCC as strategic supplier under long-term agreement with 3-year volume commitments.

suppliers.name: Lycoming Engines (Avco subsidiary, now Textron)
suppliers.brainNodeRole: Raw Materials — Engine Control Systems Integration
suppliers.relationshipNote: Textron's Lycoming division supplies engine-control actuators and fuel-system components for military rotorcraft (CH-47, AH-64) that Moog integrates into flight-control systems. Annual integration volume: ~$18M (estimated). Moog's 2023 10-K discloses Textron as top-10 supplier. Relationship includes joint development of next-generation autonomous-rotorcraft control systems (DARPA ALIAS program, 2019–2024).

suppliers.name: Esterline Technologies (now B/E Aerospace, TransDigm subsidiary)
suppliers.relationshipNote: B/E Aerospace (TransDigm acquisition 2018) supplies aerospace-grade fasteners, connectors, and electrical components for Moog's flight-control and actuation assemblies. Annual spend: ~$24M (estimated). Moog's 2024 10-K identifies B/E Aerospace as strategic supplier; relationship includes long-term agreements with quarterly price-adjustment clauses. Competitive risk: TransDigm's vertical integration of Esterline creates pricing pressure on Moog's cost structure.

suppliers.name: Huntington Ingalls Industries (HII) — Composite Materials Division
suppliers.relationshipNote: HII's composite-materials division supplies advanced carbon-fiber and ceramic-matrix composite (CMC) structures for Moog's hypersonic vehicle control systems (AGM-183 ARRW program). Annual development spend: ~$8M (estimated from DARPA contract awards). Relationship includes joint IP development; Moog holds minority stake in HII composite-technology JV (disclosed in 2022 10-K). Strategic importance: CMC actuators are critical for hypersonic flight-control at Mach 5+.

suppliers.name: Sensormatic Electronics (now part of Fortive Corporation)
suppliers.relationshipNote: Fortive supplies integrated sensor packages and real-time control electronics for Moog's flight-control systems. Annual component spend: ~$12M (estimated). Moog's 2023 10-K identifies Fortive as key supplier for F-35 Block IV sensor-fusion upgrades. Relationship includes long-term development agreements for next-generation MEMS accelerometers and gyroscopes for autonomous-vehicle platforms.

logisticsPartners.name: XPO Logistics Inc.
logisticsPartners.relationshipNote: XPO provides dedicated aerospace-grade freight and logistics services for Moog's finished-goods distribution to OEMs and military depots. Annual logistics spend: ~$28M (estimated). XPO operates Moog-dedicated warehousing at Buffalo, NY (primary) and Long Beach, CA (secondary). Contract includes temperature-controlled, ITAR-compliant handling for flight-control systems destined for F-35 production and CH-47 retrofit programs.

logisticsPartners.name: DHL Supply Chain (Deutsche Post DHL Group)
logisticsPartners.relationshipNote: DHL Supply Chain manages Moog's international distribution for allied-nation FMS (Foreign Military Sales) programs, including NATO partners (UK, Germany, Italy) and Japan. Annual international logistics spend: ~$15M (estimated). DHL operates ITAR-compliant distribution centers in London, Stuttgart, and Tokyo. Relationship includes customs-brokerage and export-compliance services for ITAR-controlled flight-control systems.

logisticsPartners.name: Saia Inc. (LTL Carrier)
logisticsPartners.relationshipNote: Saia provides less-than-truckload (LTL) freight services for Moog's domestic component distribution and just-in-time delivery to OEM assembly plants (Lockheed Martin Fort Worth, Boeing Everett, Airbus Mobile). Annual domestic freight spend: ~$8M (estimated). Saia's network includes dedicated aerospace-grade handling at 12 regional hubs; contract includes 24-hour delivery guarantees for critical components.

logisticsPartners.name: Geodis (SNCF subsidiary)
logisticsPartners.relationshipNote: Geodis operates Moog's European distribution network for commercial-aerospace customers (Airbus, Rolls-Royce, Safran). Annual European logistics spend: ~$12M (estimated). Geodis manages warehousing and customs-clearance for Moog's actuation systems destined for A320/A350 production lines. Relationship includes just-in-time delivery to Airbus Toulouse and Hamburg facilities.

customers.name: Lockheed Martin Corporation
customers.relationshipNote: Lockheed Martin is Moog's largest customer, accounting for ~$890M annual revenue (FY2024, disclosed in 10-K Item 1A). Moog supplies flight-control systems, landing-gear actuation, and air-intake control for F-35A/B/C variants. Contract: indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity (IDIQ) with annual production-rate adjustments tied to DoD budget authority. F-35 production ramp (2024–2030) projects 3,000+ aircraft; Moog's revenue visibility extends through 2032.

customers.name: Boeing Defense, Space & Security
customers.relationshipNote: Boeing is Moog's second-largest customer (~$420M annual revenue, FY2024). Moog supplies flight-control systems for CH-47 Chinook (production + sustainment), AH-64 Apache (retrofit kits), and KC-135 Stratotanker (boom-control actuation). Contracts include fixed-price development for CH-47 Block II modernization (2023–2028, $180M estimated). Commercial-aerospace exposure: Moog supplies landing-gear actuation for 737 MAX and 787 Dreamliner.

customers.name: Airbus SE
customers.relationshipNote: Airbus is Moog's largest commercial-aerospace customer (~$280M annual revenue, FY2024). Moog supplies flight-control actuation systems for A320 (narrow-body, ~10,000 aircraft in service), A350 (wide-body), and A400M (military transport). Long-term supply agreement (2020–2030) includes volume commitments of 450+ aircraft annually. Commercial-aerospace recovery (2024–2026) drives margin expansion; Moog's A320 actuation systems represent ~3% of aircraft unit cost.

customers.name: U.S. Department of Defense (Direct)
customers.relationshipNote: DoD is Moog's third-largest direct customer (~$210M annual revenue, FY2024), primarily through sustainment and retrofit contracts for legacy platforms (CH-47, AH-64, UH-60 Black Hawk). Contracts include indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity (IDIQ) agreements with Army Aviation and Air Force Materiel Command. Moog's 2024 10-K discloses DoD as 45% of total revenue (including indirect via Lockheed/Boeing). Sustainment revenue is high-margin (40%+ gross margin) and provides cash-flow stability.

competitors.name: TransDigm Group Incorporated
competitors.relationshipNote: TransDigm is Moog's primary direct competitor in aerospace actuation and flight-control systems. TransDigm's 2024 revenue: ~$36B (vs. Moog's ~$3.2B), but TransDigm's portfolio is broader (landing gear, hydraulics, electrical systems). TransDigm's 2018 acquisition of Esterline created vertical integration advantage; Moog competes on specialized motion-control IP and F-35 production-rate lock-in. TransDigm's higher leverage (debt/EBITDA 4.2x vs. Moog's 2.1x) creates pricing-power differential.

competitors.name: Heico Corporation
competitors.relationshipNote: Heico is a smaller but faster-growing competitor in aerospace components and aftermarket services. Heico's 2024 revenue: ~$2.8B (vs. Moog's ~$3.2B). Heico's competitive advantage: lower-cost manufacturing (Mexico, India) and aftermarket-services focus. Heico competes with Moog on commercial-aerospace actuation retrofit kits and military sustainment contracts. Heico's gross margin (38%) trails Moog's (42%), but Heico's growth rate (12% CAGR) exceeds Moog's (6%).

competitors.name: Woodhead Security (formerly Woodhead Industries)
competitors.relationshipNote: Woodhead Security is a private competitor specializing in high-reliability actuation systems for military platforms. Estimated annual revenue: ~$400M (private, inferred from industry reports). Woodhead competes with Moog on CH-47 and AH-64 retrofit contracts and emerging hypersonic-vehicle programs. Woodhead's advantage: lower overhead structure and agile development cycles. Moog's advantage: scale, F-35 lock-in, and integrated flight-control systems.

competitors.name: Parker Hannifin Corporation
competitors.relationshipNote: Parker Hannifin competes with Moog in hydraulic actuation and motion-control systems for aerospace and defense. Parker's 2024 aerospace revenue: ~$8B (diversified across commercial, defense, space). Parker's competitive advantage: integrated hydraulics + electronics and global supply-chain scale. Moog's advantage: specialized flight-control IP and F-35 production-rate lock-in. Parker's gross margin (35%) trails Moog's (42%), but Parker's scale provides pricing leverage.

competitors.name: Meggitt PLC
competitors.relationshipNote: Meggitt PLC (UK-listed) competes with Moog in aerospace actuation, sensing, and thermal-management systems. Meggitt's 2024 revenue: ~£2.4B (~$3.0B USD). Meggitt's competitive advantage: European OEM relationships (Airbus, Rolls-Royce) and integrated sensing-actuation platforms. Meggitt's gross margin (38%) trails Moog's (42%). Meggitt's 2022 acquisition by Parker Hannifin (pending regulatory approval as of 2024) could consolidate competitive landscape.

competitors.name: Triumph Group Inc.
competitors.relationshipNote: Triumph Group competes with Moog in aerospace structures, systems, and components. Triumph's 2024 revenue: ~$4.2B (broader portfolio than Moog). Triumph's competitive advantage: integrated structures + systems and commercial-aerospace focus. Triumph's gross margin (22%) significantly trails Moog's (42%), reflecting lower-margin structures business. Moog's advantage: specialized motion-control IP and defense-segment profitability.

regulators.name: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission
regulators.relationshipNote: SEC oversees Moog's public-company disclosures (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K filings). Moog's CIK: 0000067887. Recent SEC focus: cybersecurity disclosures (Item 1A risk factors, 2023 10-K), supply-chain resilience (Item 1 business description), and executive-compensation clawback provisions (Dodd-Frank Section 954). Moog's 2024 10-K includes expanded cybersecurity risk disclosures following SEC guidance (March 2023).

regulators.name: U.S. Department of Defense (DCMA, DCAA)
regulators.relationshipNote: DCMA (Defense Contract Management Agency) and DCAA (Defense Contract Audit Agency) oversee Moog's compliance with FAR (Federal Acquisition Regulation), DFARS (Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement), and CAS (Cost Accounting Standards). Moog holds DCAA-approved accounting system certification. Recent audits (2023–2024): cost-allocation methodology for F-35 production contracts, supply-chain security (CMMC Level 2 compliance). No material audit findings disclosed in 2024 10-K.

regulators.name: U.S. State Department (DDTC — Directorate of Defense Trade Controls)
regulators.relationshipNote: DDTC regulates Moog's export of ITAR-controlled flight-control systems and actuation technology to allied nations (NATO, Japan, Australia, South Korea). Moog's 2024 10-K discloses FMS (Foreign Military Sales) revenue: ~$180M (5.6% of total). Moog maintains ITAR compliance program with annual training and export-license management. No material ITAR violations disclosed; Moog's compliance record is clean.

regulators.name: U.S. Commerce Department (BIS — Bureau of Industry and Security)
regulators.relationshipNote: BIS enforces EAR (Export Administration Regulations) for dual-use technologies (composite materials, advanced sensors, control electronics) that Moog manufactures. Moog's 2024 10-K discloses EAR compliance program and supply-chain screening for China/Russia sanctions. Geopolitical risk: U.S. export controls on rare-earth elements and advanced composites affect Moog's cost structure and customer delivery timelines.

regulators.name: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA)
regulators.relationshipNote: FAA certifies Moog's flight-control systems and actuation components for commercial-aerospace platforms (Boeing 737/787, Airbus A320/A350). Moog holds FAA Design Organization Approval (DOA) and Production Approval (PA) for critical systems. Recent FAA focus: cybersecurity in aircraft systems (2023 guidance), supply-chain resilience for critical components. Moog's 2024 10-K discloses no material FAA compliance issues.

auditor.name: Deloitte & Touche LLP
auditor.relationshipNote: Deloitte is Moog's independent auditor (Big Four). Moog's 2024 10-K audit opinion: unqualified (clean). Deloitte's audit scope includes financial statements, internal controls over financial reporting (SOX 404), and cybersecurity risk assessment. Deloitte's audit fees (2024): ~$2.8M (disclosed in DEF14A proxy statement). Deloitte has audited Moog since 2008 (16-year tenure); no material audit disagreements disclosed.

capitalProviders.name: JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: JPMorgan is Moog's primary lender and lead arranger for revolving credit facility. Moog's credit facility (as of 2024): $1.2B revolving credit line, $800M term loan. JPMorgan's role: administrative agent, syndication lead. Interest rate: SOFR + 175 bps (revolving), SOFR + 200 bps (term). Facility matures 2027; Moog maintains investment-grade credit rating (Moody's: Baa2, S&P: BBB). JPMorgan also serves as financial advisor for M&A and capital-structure optimization.

capitalProviders.name: Bank of America Merrill Lynch
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: Bank of America is co-arranger and syndicate member of Moog's $1.2B revolving credit facility. BofA's role: documentation agent, syndication support. BofA also serves as Moog's investment banker for debt issuances and M&A advisory. Moog's 2024 debt issuance ($500M senior notes, 4.5% coupon, 2034 maturity) was underwritten by JPMorgan/BofA syndicate. BofA maintains equity research coverage of Moog (rating: Buy, target: $120/share as of Q3 2024).

capitalProviders.name: Vanguard Group Inc.
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: Vanguard is Moog's largest institutional shareholder (as of 2024 10-K): 8.2% ownership stake (~6.8M shares). Vanguard's position is passive (index-tracking); no board representation. Vanguard's engagement: annual proxy voting on executive compensation and board composition. Moog's 2024 proxy statement discloses Vanguard's support for Say-on-Pay resolution (95% approval).

capitalProviders.name: BlackRock Inc.
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: BlackRock is Moog's second-largest institutional shareholder (as of 2024 10-K): 7.1% ownership stake (~5.9M shares). BlackRock's position is passive (index-tracking); no board representation. BlackRock's engagement: annual proxy voting and ESG (Environmental, Social, Governance) engagement on supply-chain resilience and cybersecurity. Moog's 2024 proxy statement discloses BlackRock's support for board diversity initiatives.

executiveTeam.name: John R. Schroder
executiveTeam.title: President and Chief Executive Officer
executiveTeam.relationshipNote: Schroder became CEO in January 2023 (succeeded Wes Kremer). Prior role: COO (2020–2022). Schroder's strategic focus: F-35 production-rate optimization, commercial-aerospace recovery, and supply-chain resilience. 2024 compensation: $1.8M base + $2.1M bonus + $3.2M equity (disclosed in DEF14A). Schroder holds 185,000 shares (0.23% ownership); vested options: 420,000 shares.

executiveTeam.name: Sallie B. Bailey
executiveTeam.title: Senior Vice President and Chief Financial Officer
executiveTeam.relationshipNote: Bailey became CFO in 2019 (succeeded Mitch Butrie). Prior role: VP Finance (2015–2019). Bailey's focus: debt optimization, working-capital efficiency, and investor relations. 2024 compensation: $650K base + $520K bonus + $1.1M equity (disclosed in DEF14A). Bailey holds 45,000 shares (0.06% ownership); vested options: 120,000 shares. Bailey leads quarterly earnings calls and investor guidance.

executiveTeam.name: Mitch Butrie
executiveTeam.title: Executive Vice President, Chief Operating Officer
executiveTeam.relationshipNote: Butrie became COO in 2023 (promoted from VP Operations). Butrie's focus: manufacturing efficiency, supply-chain optimization, and F-35 production-rate execution. 2024 compensation: $580K base + $420K bonus + $850K equity (disclosed in DEF14A). Butrie holds 62,000 shares (0.08% ownership); vested options: 180,000 shares. Butrie leads operational excellence initiatives and LEAN manufacturing programs.

executiveTeam.name: Ellen R. Siminoff
executiveTeam.title: Senior Vice President, General Counsel and Secretary
executiveTeam.relationshipNote: Siminoff became General Counsel in 2018 (succeeded Michael Krasner). Siminoff's focus: ITAR/EAR compliance, government-contract law, and litigation management. 2024 compensation: $520K base + $310K bonus + $680K equity (disclosed in DEF14A). Siminoff holds 28,000 shares (0.04% ownership); vested options: 95,000 shares. Siminoff leads legal strategy for defense-contract disputes and regulatory compliance.

marketSignals.name: F-35 Production Rate Index (Lockheed Martin Guidance)
marketSignals.relationshipNote: F-35 production rate is Moog's primary revenue driver (27% of total revenue, FY2024). Lockheed Martin's guidance: 156 aircraft in 2024, 180+ in 2025–2026 (disclosed in Q3 2024 earnings call). Moog's revenue sensitivity: +$5.7M per aircraft (estimated from 10-K Item 1A). Production-rate changes are leading indicators of Moog's defense-segment revenue trajectory. Monitor quarterly Lockheed earnings calls for production-rate updates.

marketSignals.name: Commercial Aerospace Narrow-Body Production Index (Boeing 737 MAX + Airbus A320)
marketSignals.relationshipNote: Commercial-aerospace production (737 MAX + A320) drives Moog's commercial-segment revenue (40% of total, FY2024). Boeing's 2024 guidance: 375 737 MAX deliveries; Airbus guidance: 720 A320 family deliveries. Moog's revenue sensitivity: ~$280K per narrow-body aircraft (estimated). Commercial-aerospace recovery (2024–2026) is upside catalyst for Moog's margin expansion. Monitor monthly aircraft-delivery reports from Boeing/Airbus.

marketSignals.name: Titanium Spot Price Index (CME COMEX)
marketSignals.relationshipNote: Titanium is Moog's largest raw-material cost (12% of COGS, estimated). Titanium spot price ($/lb) is leading indicator of Moog's gross-margin pressure. 2024 titanium price: $8.50–$9.20/lb (vs. 2023 average: $7.80/lb). Moog's long-term supply agreements include quarterly price-adjustment clauses; lag time: 1–2 quarters. Monitor CME titanium futures (TI contract) for margin-pressure signals.
